title: Everyone, cheerfully (Avot 3:12)
hookLine: Rabbi Ishmael: be yielding to elders, easy with the young, and greet everyone with joy
tomorrow: silence as a fence? what's a fence doing around wisdom?

cards: Every hallway has its quick math when someone you'd rather avoid is coming: nod, smile, or suddenly find your phone fascinating. The Talmud tells a story about a teacher who never lost that race.
Of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai it says that no one ever greeted him first, not even a non-Jew in the marketplace. He always got his hello in before theirs.
Of everything a student could have remembered about a great teacher, someone kept that.

teach.b: Rabbi Ishmael puts the same instinct into one line of Avot. Its first two clauses are compact Hebrew, and translators differ; one common reading is: be yielding to those above you, and easy with the young.
Then the clause that's plain: hevei mekabel et kol ha'adam besimcha, receive every person with joy. Look at three of those words.
Mekabel is receive, more than greet: the way a host takes in a guest at the door.
Kol ha'adam is every person, every human being, not only the ones on your team or in your community.

teach.h: RECEIVE FIRST; THE FEELING CAN FOLLOW.
teach.b: That's why the marketplace detail matters: Yochanan's hello crossed the line between communities, and crossed it first. And besimcha, with joy, is the hard part. A nod is manners.
Joy says: I'm glad you're here. It's a cousin of Shammai's line in chapter one, receive every person with a cheerful face. Two teachers who argued about a great deal ended up at the same door.
Here's the honest catch: Ishmael doesn't say feel joy at everyone. Some days that feeling won't come. He says receive them that way, and lets the feeling catch up, or not.

how: Some Jews read a chapter of Pirkei Avot on Shabbat afternoons in the weeks after Passover; greeting others warmly is taught there as part of everyday Jewish ethics.

o: greeting the elders first, before the young
a cheerful mood you keep up whatever happens
receiving every person with joy, not only your own

s: Ishmael's line is about greeting your own community warmly
kol ha'adam: every person. Yochanan ben Zakkai greeted even a non-Jew in the marketplace first.
translators read Ishmael's first two clauses in more than one way
they're compact Hebrew; one common reading is yielding to elders, easy with the young.
the saying only counts if you feel joyful at everyone
it asks how you receive people; the feeling can come after.

games.q: new job, first week. the guy at the front desk never looks up when you walk in. by Ishmael's line, what's your move tomorrow?
o: greet him first, warmly, whether or not he looks up.
wait for him to say hi first, then answer warmly.
leave him be; some people just prefer to be left alone.
games.why: receive every person with joy, and like Yochanan ben Zakkai, get your hello in first.

practice: Say a hello out loud, softly, the way you'd want to be met at a door: a name, and a smile you can hear in it.
Then bring to mind the one person you're least likely to greet first tomorrow, and say it once more, to them, here where it's easy.

wordCard.voice: Everyone. Kol ha'adam in Ishmael's Hebrew: every person, received with joy, the stranger in the marketplace included.

orig.note: Hebrew: with joy, from simcha, joy; the last word of Ishmael's line.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: everyone, cheerfully, and you go first. Shalom, and see you tomorrow.

sources.q: hevei mekabel et kol ha'adam besimcha

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a (no one greeted Yochanan ben Zakkai first)
Mishnah Avot 1:15 (Shammai: receive every person with a cheerful face)
